Earth Processes · Week 4.5

Weathering, Mass Wasting & Erosion

From glaciers retreating in the high Andes to huaycos burying entire towns — Peru's landscapes are in constant motion, shaped by water, wind, gravity, and ice.

Section 1

Weathering & Mass Wasting

How Peru Experiences Weathering

Peru's extreme geographic diversity — spanning tropical rainforest, high Andean plateaus, and coastal desert — means it experiences nearly every major form of weathering simultaneously. Chemical weathering dominates in the humid Amazon basin, while physical (mechanical) weathering rules the high Andes.

Carbonation

Rainwater absorbs carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and soil, forming weak carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). In Peru's northern Andes and Amazon foothills, this acid dissolves limestone and carbonate rocks, slowly carving caves, sinkholes, and karst formations. The Cueva de las Lechuzas in Tingo María (Huánuco) is a notable example — a massive cave system carved entirely by carbonation over thousands of years.

Hydrolysis & Oxidation

In the Amazon basin, where annual rainfall exceeds 2,000–4,000 mm, hydrolysis continuously breaks down silicate minerals in granite and igneous rocks — converting feldspars into clay minerals. Oxidation is visible along riverbanks and cut slopes, where iron-bearing minerals rust and weaken rock. Together, these processes produce the thick, red-orange laterite soils common across the Peruvian jungle.

Freeze-Thaw (Frost Action)

Above 4,000 m in the Andes, temperatures regularly drop below freezing at night and rise above it during the day. Water seeps into rock fractures, freezes, expands by ~9%, and shatters the rock over time. This process — called frost wedging — is the primary agent of physical weathering in the puna (highland plateau) and produces the rugged, jagged peaks characteristic of the Cordillera Blanca.

Salt Weathering (Coastal)

Along Peru's Pacific coast, salt from sea spray and marine fog (garúa) crystallizes inside rock pores and exerts pressure that fragments rock surfaces. This form of weathering is particularly damaging to the adobe and earthen architecture of ancient Peruvian coastal cultures — it is one of the main threats to Chan Chan, the largest pre-Columbian city in South America, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Mass Wasting: Huaycos & Landslides

Peru is one of the most landslide-prone countries in South America. The steep Andean slopes, fractured rock, intense seasonal rainfall, and seismic activity create near-perfect conditions for mass wasting. The most iconic and deadly form is the huayco — a Quechua word for a fast-moving debris flow of mud, rocks, water, and organic material that surges down Andean valleys with little warning. Huaycos are triggered most often during the wet season (November–April) and amplified during El Niño events.

2017 El Niño Costero — National Disaster Costero El Niño

Between January and April 2017, an exceptionally warm El Niño Costero event caused unprecedented rainfall along Peru's normally arid Pacific coast. The result was a cascade of catastrophic huaycos and landslides across 25 of Peru's 26 regions. More than 160 people were killed, over 500,000 were directly affected, and more than 100,000 homes were damaged or destroyed. Rivers that are normally dry or shallow — including the Rímac (which supplies Lima's water) and the Piura — flooded catastrophically.

The city of Mocoa in neighboring Colombia made headlines, but within Peru, cities like Huancayo, Chosica, Trujillo, and Piura suffered widespread destruction. Roads, bridges, and critical infrastructure were swept away. The damage was estimated at over $3 billion USD, making it Peru's costliest natural disaster in decades.

1941 Huaraz Glacial Disaster GLOF + Debris Flow

On December 13, 1941, a mass of ice from the Palcacocha glacial lake above Huaraz collapsed into the lake, triggering a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) that released millions of cubic meters of water, ice, and debris. The torrent traveled 23 km down the Santa River valley and struck the city of Huaraz, killing an estimated 4,000–6,000 people — approximately one-third of the city's population at the time. This disaster prompted the first systematic glacial lake monitoring programs in the Andes.

Government Response & Risk Reduction

INDECI & Reconstrucción con Cambios

Following the 2017 El Niño Costero, the government created the Autoridad para la Reconstrucción con Cambios (ARCC), a special body tasked with rebuilding infrastructure with disaster resilience built in — including flood-resistant bridges, drainage channels, and slope stabilization works across affected regions.

CENEPRED

The Centro Nacional de Estimación, Prevención y Reducción del Riesgo de Desastres (CENEPRED) produces national hazard maps identifying landslide, huayco, and flood risk zones. Municipalities use these maps to restrict building in high-risk corridors and plan evacuation routes.

Glacial Lake Monitoring (UGRH)

The Unidad de Glaciología y Recursos Hídricos of the ANA (National Water Authority) monitors over 8,000 glacial lakes in the Cordillera Blanca. High-risk lakes like Palcacocha have drainage tunnels and automatic alert systems installed to prevent GLOF events from reaching populated valleys.

Early Warning & Reforestation

SENAMHI (Peru's national meteorological service) provides rainfall forecasts that trigger local emergency alerts. Reforestation programs with native Andean species (particularly quinual trees) are used to stabilize slopes and reduce surface runoff that triggers huaycos.

Section 2

Water Erosion & Major Rivers

Peru's River Systems

Peru is the origin of some of the world's most significant rivers. The Andes act as the great hydrological divide: rivers on the western slope flow short and fast to the Pacific, while rivers on the eastern slope feed the Amazon basin — the world's largest river system by discharge. Water erosion occurs at every scale across Peru, from splash erosion on bare slopes to canyon-carving river incision thousands of meters deep.

Amazon River (Río Amazonas)

Source: Nevado Mismi, Arequipa (~5,597 m) · Length: ~6,400 km · Discharge: ~209,000 m³/s

Largest River by Volume

The Amazon River — the world's largest river by water discharge — has its most distant source at Nevado Mismi, a glaciated peak in the Arequipa region of Peru. Within Peru, the river is known as the Ucayali-Amazon system and flows generally northeastward before crossing into Colombia and Brazil. Its delta (actually an estuary) empties into the Atlantic Ocean near Marajó Island in Brazil.

In its lower Peruvian reaches (around Iquitos), the Amazon displays classic meandering behavior — wide, sweeping bends that constantly migrate laterally through erosion on outer banks and deposition on inner banks (point bars). Oxbow lakes (cochas) are abundant throughout the Peruvian Amazon, formed when meanders are cut off. River erosion along the Amazon's banks is gradual but constant, reshaping floodplains and displacing riverside communities.

Ucayali River (Río Ucayali)

Source: Apurímac River confluence · Length: ~1,771 km · Major tributary of the Amazon

Meandering

The Ucayali is one of the two main headwater rivers of the Amazon and flows entirely within Peru. Its upper course (formed by the Urubamba and Apurímac rivers) is steep and fast — with braided channels and high sediment loads from the Andes. As it descends into the lowland Amazon basin around Pucallpa, it transitions into a strongly meandering river with an enormous floodplain. Lateral erosion here can shift the river channel by several hundred meters per year, threatening towns, indigenous territories, and agricultural land.

Marañón River (Río Marañón)

Source: Lake Lauricocha, Huánuco · Length: ~1,800 km · Discharges into Amazon

Canyon-Cutting

The Marañón is Peru's second major Amazon headwater. It is remarkable for cutting some of the deepest river gorges in South America — in the Pongo de Manseriche canyon, it drops through a narrow Andean gorge before entering the Amazon lowlands. The upper Marañón has a straight to braided channel pattern due to steep gradients and high coarse sediment supply. The river plays a critical role in erosion: it transports millions of tons of sediment annually from the Andes to the Amazon floodplain, building Peru's fertile várzea (seasonally flooded forest) ecosystems.

Rímac River (Río Rímac)

Source: Cordillera Occidental, ~5,500 m · Length: ~160 km · Estuary: Pacific Ocean at Callao

High Erosion Risk

The Rímac is Peru's most economically critical river — it supplies drinking water to over 10 million people in Lima and Callao. Despite being relatively short, it drops over 5,000 meters in elevation, giving it extreme erosive power in its upper reaches. The Rímac's channel is largely straight to slightly braided in the highland sections, cutting deeply into volcanic and sedimentary rock. During the 2017 El Niño Costero, the Rímac flooded critically and carried massive amounts of sediment and debris into Lima, contaminating water supplies for weeks and destroying bridges in the Chosica and San Juan de Lurigancho districts.

Economic & Social Impacts of River Erosion

Threat to Agriculture

Lateral erosion along the Amazon and Ucayali floods and destroys agricultural plots that riverside communities depend on for subsistence. In the Ucayali region, entire village riverbanks have collapsed into the river, forcing repeated relocations of indigenous communities.

Infrastructure Destruction

Streambank erosion regularly destroys roads and bridges in Andean valleys. The Carretera Central — Peru's main highway connecting Lima to the central Andes — runs alongside the Rímac River and suffers recurrent damage from floods and bank erosion, disrupting commerce and supply chains.

Water Security

High sediment loads from erosion clog reservoirs, reduce water storage capacity, and overwhelm treatment plants. Lima's water utility (SEDAPAL) faces growing costs as erosion upstream from the Rímac increases turbidity in the water supply.

Loss of Floodplain Settlements

Rapid urbanization has pushed millions of Peruvians into high-risk floodplain zones. In cities like Iquitos and Pucallpa, informal settlements built on river margins are constantly threatened by seasonal flooding and bank erosion, displacing thousands annually.

Government Mitigation Measures

  • ANA (Autoridad Nacional del Agua) manages river basin plans and sets restrictions on floodplain development.
  • Dike and retaining wall construction along the Rímac and Santa rivers to reduce bank erosion and protect adjacent communities.
  • Reforestation of river headwaters under programs like Siembra y Cosecha de Agua to reduce runoff and sediment delivery to rivers.
  • Early flood warning systems along the Piura and Santa rivers using automated river gauges that alert downstream communities.
Section 3

Wind Erosion

Aeolian Processes Along Peru's Coast

Yes — wind erosion is a significant process in Peru, particularly along its 2,414 km Pacific coastline and in the highland puna zones. Peru's coastal desert is one of the driest on Earth, with almost no vegetation to bind sediment. The prevailing south and southwest winds drive persistent aeolian (wind-driven) activity, transporting fine sand and silty materials from exposed beaches, riverbeds, and dry coastal plains.

Coastal Dune Migration

Peru's coast hosts extensive barchan dunes — crescent-shaped dunes that migrate inland at rates of 10–20 meters per year. These are particularly visible near Ica, Nazca, Paracas, and Lima's southern districts. The famous oasis of Huacachina (near Ica) is entirely surrounded by massive sand dunes shaped by persistent coastal winds. Migrating dunes have encroached on farmland, roads, and even archaeological sites in the Nazca region.

Deflation on the Altiplano

On the high Andean altiplano (above 3,800 m), the thin, dry soils and sparse vegetation are vulnerable to deflation — wind removing fine particles from the surface. Strong winds that funnel through Andean valleys carry dust that blankets glacier surfaces, accelerating melting. In the Puno and Arequipa regions, overgrazing has removed vegetation cover, greatly increasing the rate of wind erosion from highland soils.

Government Mitigation

Windbreaks & Afforestation

Peru's SERFOR (National Forest and Wildlife Service) promotes planting of native trees along coastal roads and agricultural edges to act as windbreaks. In the Ica region, rows of eucalyptus and tamarisk are used to slow wind and anchor sand dunes near productive farmland.

Dune Stabilization

The Ministry of Environment has funded experimental dune-stabilization projects using native coastal plants (totora, achupalla) to bind sand and prevent migration toward road infrastructure. Sand fencing is also used in areas adjacent to the Pan-American Highway.

Highland Revegetation

In Andean puna zones affected by deflation and overgrazing, reforestation with ichu grasses and quinual trees is promoted. AGRORURAL (a rural development agency) supports Andean communities in rotating grazing pastures to allow vegetation recovery and reduce wind erosion.

Section 4

Deserts & Desertification

Peru's Deserts

Peru's Pacific coast is one of the driest places on Earth. The extreme aridity is caused by two intersecting factors: the Humboldt (Peru) Current, which flows northward along the coast and cools the overlying air — preventing it from rising, condensing, and producing rain — and the rain shadow effect of the Andes, which blocks moisture from the Amazon. As a result, Lima receives an average of only 8–10 mm of rainfall per year.

Sechura Desert

Erg (sand dunes) Reg (gravel plains)

Location: Piura & Lambayeque regions, northern coast · Area: ~188,000 km²

The Sechura Desert is Peru's largest desert and one of the most arid zones in South America. It extends across the northern coastal plain and contains both erg landscapes (vast seas of sand dunes, especially near the Bayóvar Peninsula) and reg landscapes (flat, stony gravel plains where wind has stripped away fine particles). The desert is bisected by short rivers flowing from the Andes that occasionally reach the sea, creating narrow oasis corridors used for agriculture. It is economically significant for its phosphate deposits (among the largest in the world) and offshore fishing.

Atacama Desert (Southern Extension into Peru)

Hamada (bare rock) Reg (gravel)

Location: Extends from Chile into the Tacna & Moquegua regions of southern Peru

The Atacama — the world's driest non-polar desert — extends into Peru's southernmost coastal regions. In these areas, landscapes are predominantly hamada (exposed bedrock, swept clean of fine sediment by wind) and reg (coarse gravel plains). There is almost no biological soil crust or vegetation. This southern Peruvian desert zone hosts important archaeological sites including the Nazca Lines, whose preservation over thousands of years is largely due to the extreme aridity and absence of weathering agents.

Coastal Lomas Ecosystems

Fog-Dependent Life

Between the coastal deserts, Peru has unique lomas ecosystems — fog oases where dense Pacific marine fog (garúa) condenses on hillslopes and supports seasonal plant communities despite receiving virtually no rain. These fragile ecosystems appear green during the austral winter fog season (June–November) but are extremely vulnerable to human disturbance.

Is Desertification a Growing Problem?

Yes. While Peru's coastal deserts are naturally hyperarid, desertification — the degradation of dryland soils driven by human activity and climate variability — is an increasing concern, particularly in three zones:

Andean Highlands (Puna)

Overgrazing by cattle, sheep, and alpacas in the puna and sierra zones has degraded vast areas of highland grassland. Without root systems to hold soil, wind and water erosion accelerate, progressively turning productive pasturelands into bare, eroded terrain. The Ayacucho and Puno regions are most affected.

Dry Inter-Andean Valleys

The dry valleys between Andean ranges (like the Mantaro and Apurímac valleys) experience semi-arid conditions that are worsening with deforestation. Steep slopes, combined with intensive agriculture and removal of native vegetation, accelerate rill and gully erosion.

Coastal Irrigation Zones

Intensive irrigated agriculture in coastal valleys has led to soil salinization — a form of desertification where salt accumulates in soil due to poor drainage, reducing agricultural productivity. The Ica and Piura valleys are experiencing significant groundwater depletion and soil salinity increases.

The Peruvian government ratified the UN Convention to Combat Desertification (UNCCD) and has developed a National Action Plan against Desertification. Programs focus on sustainable land management, terracing (andenes), agroforestry, and recovery of traditional Andean soil conservation techniques.

Section 5

Glaciers

Peru's Glaciers: A Rapidly Shrinking Resource

Peru holds approximately 68% of the world's tropical glaciers — a remarkable concentration of ice in the Andes between latitudes 8°S and 18°S. These glaciers exist because of the extreme altitude (most above 5,000 m) rather than the latitude. However, since the 1970s, Peru has lost over 50% of its glacier surface area due to rising temperatures driven by climate change. This loss has profound implications for Peru's water security, energy generation, agriculture, and indigenous cultures.

Quelccaya Ice Cap

~5,680 m · Cusco Region

Largest Tropical Ice Cap

The Quelccaya Ice Cap is the world's largest tropical glacier, covering approximately 44 km² (down from ~60 km² in 1975). Located in the Cusco region at the edge of the Amazon basin, it is one of the most scientifically studied glaciers on Earth. Ice cores from Quelccaya have provided a 1,500-year climate record for the tropics (Thompson et al., 1985). Since the 1980s, its retreat has accelerated dramatically — glaciologist Lonnie Thompson has documented its fastest rates of retreat in the entire ice core record. The glacier supplies meltwater to the Vilcanota River system, which feeds agriculture and hydropower in the Cusco and Puno regions.

Pastoruri Glacier

~5,240 m · Ancash Region

Critical Retreat

Once a popular tourist destination in Huascarán National Park, Pastoruri Glacier has retreated so dramatically that it was reclassified from a glacier to a "glacieret" (a very small glacier body). Between 1990 and 2010, it lost approximately 40% of its surface area. The Peruvian government converted this loss into a climate change education opportunity — Pastoruri is now the centerpiece of the Ruta del Cambio Climático (Climate Change Route), a tourism circuit that brings visitors to witness glacier retreat firsthand and understand its local consequences.

Cordillera Blanca Glaciers

Ancash Region · 722 glaciers

Most Glaciated Tropical Range

The Cordillera Blanca ("White Range") in Ancash is the most extensively glaciated tropical mountain range on Earth, with over 700 individual glaciers covering Huascarán (6,768 m) and dozens of adjacent peaks. The glaciers feed the Santa River — source of the Chavimochic irrigation project that supplies water to over 100,000 hectares of farmland on the La Libertad coast. Studies by Peru's glaciology unit (UGRH) show the Cordillera Blanca lost approximately 27% of its glacier area between 1970 and 2003, with acceleration since then.

Ancient & Remaining Glacial Features

U-Shaped Valleys

During the Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 years ago), glaciers extended far lower than today. Their slow movement carved the characteristic U-shaped valleys visible throughout the Cordillera Blanca and Huancavelica regions. The Callejón de Huaylas — the broad, flat-bottomed valley in Ancash — is a classic glacially carved trough, now densely populated and agriculturally productive because glacial erosion left behind fertile, flat valley floors.

Glacial Lakes (Lagunas)

Peru has over 8,000 glacial lakes (lagunas) — formed when retreating glaciers leave behind hollows blocked by moraine deposits. While many are scenic (Laguna 69, Humantay Lake), some pose serious GLOF (Glacial Lake Outburst Flood) hazards. Palcacocha Lake above Huaraz has been artificially drained and fitted with drainage infrastructure after the catastrophic 1941 outburst flood that killed thousands.

Moraines

Lateral and terminal moraines — ridges of rock and sediment deposited by glaciers — are common throughout the Peruvian Andes. Ancient moraines at lower elevations mark the extent of past glacial advances. They are important for hydrological research and are increasingly used to reconstruct paleoclimate and understand how Peru's water resources are changing as glaciers retreat above their historical moraine limits.

Impact on Water & Energy

Glacier meltwater currently buffers river flows during dry seasons — as glaciers shrink, dry-season river flows will initially increase (from accelerated melt) then eventually decline dramatically. This "peak water" problem threatens Lima's water supply, the Chavimochic irrigation project, and Peru's hydroelectric dams — which generate ~60% of the country's electricity. The ANA estimates that by 2050, many coastal rivers will lose 30–40% of dry-season flow as glaciers disappear.

Watch: Peru's Vanishing Glaciers

Peru holds 68% of the world's tropical glaciers — and is losing them at an alarming rate. This video illustrates the real-world impact of glacial retreat in the Andes: shrinking water supplies, increased landslide risk from destabilized slopes, and communities adapting to a landscape shaped by thousands of years of ice that is now disappearing within a single lifetime.
